questions.question: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) — Clean Boundaries
questions.title: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) — Clean Boundaries
questions.direct_answer: Hexagonal Architecture (also called Ports and Adapters) structures an application so that the core business logic has zero dependencies on frameworks, databases, or external systems. The core defines 'ports' — interfaces that describe what it needs — and 'adapters' implement those interfaces using specific technologies. You can swap PostgreSQL for MongoDB, REST for gRPC, or replace any external system by writing a new adapter without touching business logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the inversion — that the domain defines what it needs via ports, and infrastructure conforms to those ports, not the other way around
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Hexagonal as just 'use interfaces everywhere' without understanding that the direction of dependency is the point — the domain never imports infrastructure packages
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the distinction between driving ports (inbound — API calls trigger use cases) and driven ports (outbound — use cases request external resources), and explain how Spring DI wires adapters to ports at runtime

sections.title: When Your Framework Becomes Your Domain's Landlord
sections.content:
In a typical Spring Boot application after a year of development, open any Service class and count the imports. You'll find `@Entity` annotations from JPA, `@JsonProperty` from Jackson, `@Cacheable` from Spring, maybe an `@KafkaListener`. The business logic is tangled with infrastructure assumptions. Testing the Service requires a running database because domain objects ARE JPA entities. Swapping PostgreSQL for MongoDB means rewriting business logic classes because persistence annotations are embedded in them.

This happens because the **dependency direction is wrong.** The domain depends on infrastructure — JPA, Spring, Kafka — instead of the other way around.

**Hexagonal Architecture inverts this.** The domain core defines **ports** — interfaces that describe what it needs. "I need to save an order" becomes `OrderPersistencePort`. "I need to send a notification" becomes `NotificationPort`. Infrastructure code provides **adapters** — concrete implementations that fulfill those ports. A JPA adapter saves orders to PostgreSQL. A Kafka adapter publishes notifications to a topic. A mock adapter returns test data.

The result is a domain core with zero framework imports. No `@Entity`, no `@Component`, no `@RestController`, no `@JsonProperty`. The domain compiles and tests with nothing but the JDK. Spring Boot, JPA, Kafka — everything — lives in adapter packages that plug into the domain's ports. Swapping any external system means writing a new adapter. The business logic never changes.

sections.title: Driving Ports: How the Outside World Triggers Business Logic
Driven Ports: How Business Logic Reaches the Outside World
Making Boundaries Enforceable: Package Structure and ArchUnit
sections.content:
Hexagonal boundaries are only as strong as the enforcement mechanism. If domain classes and adapters live in the same package — or even adjacent packages with no import restrictions — someone will import a JPA annotation in a domain class during a deadline crunch. The boundary erodes silently.

The standard package structure physically separates the hexagon:

```
com.example.order/
├── domain/              # Zero framework imports — pure Java
│   ├── model/           # Order, OrderId, Money (plain POJOs)
│   ├── port/
│   │   ├── in/          # PlaceOrderUseCase, CancelOrderUseCase
│   │   └── out/         # OrderPersistencePort, NotificationPort
│   └── service/         # PlaceOrderService implements PlaceOrderUseCase
└── infrastructure/      # All framework code
    ├── web/             # OrderRestAdapter (@RestController)
    ├── persistence/     # JpaOrderAdapter, OrderEntity, JpaOrderRepository
    └── messaging/       # KafkaNotificationAdapter
```

To make this enforceable at build time — not just via code review that people skip under pressure — add an **ArchUnit** test:

```java
@ArchTest
static final ArchRule domainMustNotDependOnInfrastructure =
    noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
        .should().dependOnClassesThat()
        .resideInAPackage("..infrastructure..");
```

This runs in CI. If anyone imports a Spring or JPA class inside the domain package, the build fails with a clear error message naming the offending import. This transforms an architectural principle into an automated guardrail. Without ArchUnit or a similar tool, hexagonal boundaries in any codebase with more than two contributors erode within months.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **The domain defines ports, infrastructure provides adapters** — dependency direction is always inward. The domain package has zero imports from Spring, JPA, Jackson, or any framework. If you see `@Entity` in the domain, the architecture is violated
- **Driving (inbound) ports vs driven (outbound) ports** — driving ports define use cases triggered by controllers, CLI, events; driven ports define external resources the domain needs (persistence, messaging). Both are interfaces in the domain package
- **Adapter mapping prevents entity leakage** — JPA `@Entity` classes exist only inside the persistence adapter. The adapter maps between JPA entities and plain domain objects at the boundary. Schema changes never propagate to business logic
- **ArchUnit enforces boundaries at build time** — `noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..infrastructure..")` catches violations in CI. Without automated enforcement, boundaries erode under deadline pressure
- **Spring DI is the wiring mechanism** — constructor injection connects ports to adapters at runtime. In tests, inject mock adapters. The domain code is identical in production and in test — only the adapters differ

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Hexagonal Architecture solves a dependency problem that builds up gradually. In most Spring Boot apps, the domain becomes hostage to frameworks — JPA annotations on domain objects, Spring annotations in business logic, Jackson on DTOs that carry business rules. Swapping the database or upgrading the framework touches business code.

The fix is **dependency inversion.** The domain defines **ports** — interfaces describing what it needs. `OrderPersistencePort` says "I need to save an order" without naming JPA or PostgreSQL. **Adapters** in the infrastructure layer implement those ports using specific technologies.

There are two kinds. **Driving ports** are inbound — `PlaceOrderUseCase` defines what the app can do. Controllers, GraphQL resolvers, and event consumers are driving adapters that call these ports. **Driven ports** are outbound — `OrderPersistencePort` defines what the app needs. JPA repositories, Kafka producers, and HTTP clients are driven adapters that implement these ports.

The practical payoff is testability and replaceability. The domain compiles with the JDK alone — no Spring context, no database. You test use cases by injecting mock adapters. Swapping PostgreSQL for MongoDB means writing a new persistence adapter without touching business logic.

I enforce boundaries with **ArchUnit** — a build-time test that fails if any domain class imports an infrastructure class. Without automated enforcement, the boundary erodes within months in any team under delivery pressure.

questions.question: What is the Ports and Adapters (Hexagonal Architecture) pattern and how does it relate to Clean Architecture?
questions.title: Ports and Adapters — Hexagonal Architecture
questions.direct_answer: Hexagonal Architecture, coined by Alistair Cockburn, places the application at the center surrounded by ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations). Ports define how the outside world communicates with the application (driving ports) or how the application communicates with external systems (driven ports). Clean Architecture is a refinement of this idea, adding more granularity with its concentric layer model.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of Clean Architecture and how multiple architectural styles relate to each other
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating ports and adapters as just a naming convention rather than understanding the inversion of control they enforce
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish primary (driving) adapters from secondary (driven) adapters and map them to concrete Spring Boot components

sections.title: Beyond Naming: The Inversion That Hexagonal Architecture Actually Enforces
sections.content:
Think of your application as a house with many doors. Each door is a standardized opening — the house doesn't care whether a person, a robot, or a delivery drone walks through it. The door is the **port** (a standard interface), and whoever walks through it is the **adapter** (a specific implementation). Replace the person with a robot, the house doesn't change. Add a new door on the back wall, the house's internal rooms don't change either.

Alistair Cockburn designed Hexagonal Architecture around this symmetry. The application core defines ports — interfaces that describe what interactions are possible — and the outside world provides adapters that plug into those ports. The hexagon shape isn't about having six sides; it's about having **multiple symmetric entry and exit points**, breaking the top-down mental model of layered architecture where REST is always at the top and the database always at the bottom.

The common misconception is that "ports and adapters" is just a fancy naming convention for interfaces and implementations. It's actually a **structural inversion**: the application core defines the contract, and external systems adapt to it — not the other way around. This is the same dependency inversion that Clean Architecture enforces, expressed through different terminology.

sections.title: Primary (Driving) Side — Who Calls Your Application
Secondary (Driven) Side — What Your Application Calls Out To
How Hexagonal Maps to Clean Architecture — Same Principle, Different Granularity
sections.content:
Hexagonal Architecture and Clean Architecture are different lenses on the same principle: **the application core defines contracts, external systems adapt to them**. The mapping is direct: input ports are Use Case interfaces, output ports are repository and gateway interfaces, primary adapters are controllers and CLI commands, secondary adapters are JPA repositories and API clients.

Clean Architecture adds explicit granularity that Hexagonal doesn't prescribe. It separates Entities (enterprise rules) from Use Cases (application rules) and distinguishes Interface Adapters from Frameworks & Drivers. Hexagonal treats everything inside the hexagon as "the core" without subdividing it. For teams that want more structure inside the core, Clean Architecture's concentric layers provide that. For teams that just want the outside-in inversion without internal layer rules, Hexagonal is sufficient.

In practice, most Spring Boot projects blend both vocabularies. They say "port" when talking about interfaces and "layer" when talking about package structure. The terms are complementary, not competing — and an interviewer asking about both is testing whether you understand the shared principle behind the different naming.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hexagon = symmetry, not six sides** — the shape communicates that REST, CLI, Kafka, and tests are all equal entry/exit points, breaking the "REST on top, DB on bottom" mental model
- **Primary adapters call in, secondary adapters are called** — a `@RestController` is a driving adapter translating HTTP to use case calls; `JpaOrderRepository` is a driven adapter implementing a domain port
- **Ports are owned by the application core** — `OrderRepository` and `PaymentGateway` interfaces live inside the hexagon; external systems adapt to the core's vocabulary, not the reverse
- **Pluggable testing without framework overhead** — swap `StripePaymentAdapter` for `FakePaymentGateway` implementing the same port; interactor tests run without network, database, or Spring context
- **Clean Architecture refines Hexagonal** — same inversion principle with explicit inner subdivisions (Entities → Use Cases); teams often blend both vocabularies in practice

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Hexagonal Architecture and Clean Architecture express the same fundamental idea: your business logic defines the interfaces, and everything external adapts to them. Hexagonal uses the hexagon metaphor — not because six sides matter, but to communicate that your application has many **symmetric entry and exit points**. REST, CLI, Kafka, scheduled jobs — they all plug in the same way.

The structure splits into two sides. **Primary adapters** drive your application — a `@RestController` translates HTTP into a call on an input port like `PlaceOrderUseCase`. **Secondary adapters** are driven by your application — a `JpaOrderRepository` implements the output port `OrderRepository` that the use case defines. Both port types are owned by the application core, which means external systems adapt to your vocabulary, not the other way around.

The distinction from Clean Architecture is granularity, not principle. Hexagonal treats the inside of the hexagon as one unit. Clean Architecture subdivides it into Entities and Use Cases with their own dependency rules. In practice, most teams use both vocabularies — "ports" when discussing interface contracts and "layers" when discussing package structure.

The practical test is simple: can you run your interactor with a fake payment gateway and an in-memory repository? If yes, you have genuine hexagonal boundaries. If you need a running Stripe sandbox and PostgreSQL just to test order validation, the ports are leaking infrastructure.
